claim: IFITM proteins belong to the Dispanin/CD225 family.
source: The interferon-inducible transmembrane (IFITM) proteins belong to the Dispanin/CD225 family and inhibit diverse virus infections.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: IFITM proteins inhibit diverse virus infections.
source: The interferon-inducible transmembrane (IFITM) proteins belong to the Dispanin/CD225 family and inhibit diverse virus infections.
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: IFITM3 reduces membrane fusion between cells and virions.
source: IFITM3 reduces membrane fusion between cells and virions through a poorly characterized mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mutation of PRRT2 at glycine-305 is linked to paroxysmal neurological disorders in humans.
source: Mutation of proline-rich transmembrane protein 2 (PRRT2), a regulator of neurotransmitter release, at glycine-305 was previously linked to paroxysmal neurological disorders in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Glycine-305 in PRRT2 and glycine-95 in IFITM3 drive protein oligomerization from within a GxxxG motif.
source: Here, we show that glycine-305 and the homologous site in IFITM3, glycine-95, drive protein oligomerization from within a GxxxG motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: Mutation of glycine-95 disrupts IFITM3 oligomerization.
source: Mutation of glycine-95 (and to a lesser extent, glycine-91) disrupted IFITM3 oligomerization and reduced its antiviral activity against Influenza A virus.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data in Figure 4 and co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5.

claim: Mutation of glycine-95 reduces IFITM3 antiviral activity against Influenza A virus.
source: Mutation of glycine-95 (and to a lesser extent, glycine-91) disrupted IFITM3 oligomerization and reduced its antiviral activity against Influenza A virus.
evidence: This is supported by infection assays shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: IFITM3 promotes membrane rigidity in a glycine-95-dependent manner.
source: An oligomerization-defective variant was used to reveal that IFITM3 promotes membrane rigidity in a glycine-95-dependent and amphipathic helix-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR and Laurdan measurements shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFITM3 promotes membrane rigidity in an amphipathic helix-dependent manner.
source: An oligomerization-defective variant was used to reveal that IFITM3 promotes membrane rigidity in a glycine-95-dependent and amphipathic helix-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Amphotericin B prevents IFITM3-mediated rigidification of membranes.
source: Furthermore, a compound which counteracts virus inhibition by IFITM3, Amphotericin B, prevented the IFITM3-mediated rigidification of membranes.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IFITM3 oligomers inhibit virus-cell fusion by promoting membrane rigidity.
source: Overall, these data suggest that IFITM3 oligomers inhibit virus-cell fusion by promoting membrane rigidity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including oligomerization assays, membrane order measurements, and antiviral activity assays.

claim: IFITM3 is a potent inhibitor of Influenza A virus infection in cell culture and in vivo.
source: IFITM3 is a potent inhibitor of Influenza A virus (IAV) infection in cell culture and in vivo, and consequently, it is the most studied member of the IFITM family (Bailey et al., 2012; Everitt et al., 2012; Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 inhibits virus-cell fusion by restricting fusion pore formation during virus-cell membrane fusion.
source: The interferon-induced transmembrane (IFITM) proteins are the earliest acting restriction factors known, inhibiting the entry of diverse viruses into cells by restricting fusion pore formation during virus-cell membrane fusion (Shi et al., 2017; Chesarino et al., 2014a; Perreira et al., 2013; Bailey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM proteins inhibit orthomyxoviruses, flaviviruses, filoviruses, alphaviruses, and coronaviruses.
source: Among the growing list of viruses shown to be inhibited by IFITM proteins in cell culture and in vivo are orthomyxoviruses, flaviviruses, filoviruses, alphaviruses, and coronaviruses (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: IFITM3 plays an indirect role by interacting with VAPA and inhibiting lipid transport between the endoplasmic reticulum and endosomes.
source: In the first, IFITM3 plays an indirect role by interacting with VAMP-associated protein A (VAPA) and inhibiting lipid transport between the endoplasmic reticulum and endosomes, resulting in an accumulation of endosomal cholesterol (Amini-Bavil-Olyaee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a model proposed by previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: The VAPA-cholesterol model of IFITM3 function has been challenged by several studies.
source: While inhibition of cholesterol trafficking has been shown to inhibit virus entry (Poh et al., 2012), this model of IFITM3 function has been subsequently supported by one study (Kühnl et al., 2018) but challenged by several others (Appourchaux et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2013; Desai et al., 2014; Wrensch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: IFITM3 directly inhibits fusion by locally reducing membrane fluidity.
source: The second and currently favored model posits that IFITM3 directly inhibits fusion by locally reducing membrane fluidity (i.e. increasing membrane rigidity or order) (Lin et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013) and by inducing positive membrane curvature (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 induces positive membrane curvature.
source: The second and currently favored model posits that IFITM3 directly inhibits fusion by locally reducing membrane fluidity (i.e. increasing membrane rigidity or order) (Lin et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013) and by inducing positive membrane curvature (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Membrane order and curvature influence one another.
source: Membrane order and curvature influence one another (Vanni et al., 2014; Rangamani et al., 2014; Golani et al., 2019) and, together, they regulate numerous membrane fusion processes (Martens and McMahon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 contains a juxtamembrane amphipathic helix which is essential for antiviral activity.
source: Consistent with the notion that IFITM3 induces local membrane order and curvature to disfavor virus-cell fusion, IFITM3 contains a juxtamembrane amphipathic helix which is essential for antiviral activity (Chesarino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Amphipathic helices are well known for their ability to bind and bend membranes.
source: Amphipathic helices have been identified in many eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral proteins and are well known for their ability to bind and bend membranes (Drin and Antonny, 2010; Giménez-Andrés et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 incorporated into enveloped viruses impairs virion fusion with target cells.
source: Another piece of evidence that supports the membrane deformation model of fusion inhibition is that IFITM3 incorporated into enveloped viruses also impairs virion fusion with target cells (Tartour et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2015; Tartour et al., 2017; Ahi et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2019; Compton et al., 2016; Suddala et al., 2019; Compton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 forms clusters on virus-containing vesicles.
source: It was previously reported that IFITM3 forms clusters on virus-containing vesicles (Kummer et al., 2019) and that IFITM3 oligomerization promotes restriction of IAV (John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phenylalanines at residues 75 and 78 of the CD225 domain are unnecessary for IFITM3 oligomerization when measured using FRET in living cells.
source: However, the determinants initially purported to mediate oligomerization (phenylalanines at residues 75 and 78 of the CD225 domain [John et al., 2013]) were later shown to be unnecessary when oligomerization was measured using a FRET-based approach in living cells (Winkler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The IFITM genes are members of the Dispanin/CD225 family.
source: The IFITM genes (IFITM1, IFITM2, IFITM3, IFITM5, and IFITM10 in humans) are members of an extended gene family known as the Dispanin/CD225 family (hereafter referred to as CD225 proteins) (Sällman Almén et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Members of the CD225 family are characterized by the presence of a CD225 domain.
source: Members of this group are characterized by the presence of a CD225 domain, but the functions of most remain unknown.
evidence: This is a general statement about the CD225 family.

claim: Mutations in PRRT2 result in paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, benign familial infantile seizures, and episodic ataxia.
source: Mutations in proline-rich transmembrane protein 2 (PRRT2) result in conditions of involuntary movement, such as paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, benign familial infantile seizures, and episodic ataxia (Gardiner et al., 2015; Valtorta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PRRT2 is a neuron-specific protein localized to pre-synaptic terminals.
source: PRRT2 is a neuron-specific protein that is localized to pre-synaptic terminals and which inhibits synaptic vesicle fusion (Meschia, 2018; Mo et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PRRT2 inhibits synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: PRRT2 is a neuron-specific protein that is localized to pre-synaptic terminals and which inhibits synaptic vesicle fusion (Meschia, 2018; Mo et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disease-associated missense mutations in PRRT2 (G305W/R) cause loss-of-function, leading to unchecked neurotransmitter release.
source: Molecular studies of disease-associated missense mutations in PRRT2 (G305W/R) indicate that it causes loss-of-function, leading to unchecked neurotransmitter release (Valente et al., 2016; Coleman et al., 2018; Gardiner et al., 2012; van Vliet et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The homologous residue to PRRT2 G305 in human IFITM3 is glycine-95.
source: Interestingly, the homologous residue in human IFITM3 is also subject to rare allelic variation in humans (G95W/R) and this mutation results in partial loss of activity against IAV infection (John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The G95W/R mutation in IFITM3 results in partial loss of activity against IAV infection.
source: Interestingly, the homologous residue in human IFITM3 is also subject to rare allelic variation in humans (G95W/R) and this mutation results in partial loss of activity against IAV infection (John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Glycine-95 of human IFITM3 resides within a GxxxG motif that is highly conserved among vertebrate IFITM3 orthologs and PRRT2.
source: Here, we demonstrate that glycine-95 of human IFITM3 resides within a GxxxG motif that is highly conserved among vertebrate IFITM3 orthologs as well as PRRT2.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignments shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Mutation of glycine-91 or glycine-95 renders IFITM3 less active against IAV in target cells.
source: Mutation of glycine-91 or glycine-95 rendered IFITM3 less active against IAV (in target cells) and HIV-1 (in virus-producing cells).
evidence: This is supported by infection assays shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Mutation of glycine-91 or glycine-95 renders IFITM3 less active against HIV-1 in virus-producing cells.
source: Mutation of glycine-91 or glycine-95 rendered IFITM3 less active against IAV (in target cells) and HIV-1 (in virus-producing cells).
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The GxxxG motif mediates IFITM3 oligomerization in living cells, with glycine-95 playing a dominant role.
source: We found that the GxxxG motif mediates IFITM3 oligomerization in living cells, with glycine-95 playing a dominant role.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: IFITM3 G95L mutant is deficient for oligomerization.
source: An IFITM3 mutant (G95L) exhibiting loss of antiviral function was deficient for oligomerization, indicating that IFITM3 oligomerization and virus restriction are functionally associated.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data in Figure 4 and co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5.

claim: IFITM3 oligomerization and virus restriction are functionally associated.
source: An IFITM3 mutant (G95L) exhibiting loss of antiviral function was deficient for oligomerization, indicating that IFITM3 oligomerization and virus restriction are functionally associated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between oligomerization defects and loss of antiviral activity.

claim: IFITM3 WT increases membrane order.
source: We found that IFITM3 increased membrane order, as previously suggested, whereas IFITM3 encoding G95L or mutations within its amphipathic helix failed to do so.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR and Laurdan measurements shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFITM3 G95L fails to increase membrane order.
source: We found that IFITM3 increased membrane order, as previously suggested, whereas IFITM3 encoding G95L or mutations within its amphipathic helix failed to do so.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR and Laurdan measurements shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFITM3 with mutations in its amphipathic helix fails to increase membrane order.
source: We found that IFITM3 increased membrane order, as previously suggested, whereas IFITM3 encoding G95L or mutations within its amphipathic helix failed to do so.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Amphotericin B decreases the stiffness of IFITM3-containing membranes.
source: In an effort to further probe the importance of membrane order in the antiviral mechanism, we demonstrate that Amphotericin B (Ampho B) decreases the stiffness of IFITM3-containing membranes and rescues virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Amphotericin B rescues virus infection in IFITM3-expressing cells.
source: In an effort to further probe the importance of membrane order in the antiviral mechanism, we demonstrate that Amphotericin B (Ampho B) decreases the stiffness of IFITM3-containing membranes and rescues virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by infection assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Promotion of membrane order by IFITM3 oligomers is required for its antiviral activity.
source: These data indicate that promotion of membrane order by IFITM3 oligomers is required for its antiviral activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between oligomerization, membrane order, and antiviral activity.

claim: Oligomerization is a shared requirement for the distinct anti-fusion functions performed by homologs IFITM3 and PRRT2.
source: Furthermore, we reveal that oligomerization is a shared requirement for the distinct anti-fusion functions performed by homologs IFITM3 and PRRT2.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data for PRRT2 shown in Figure 7.

claim: IFITM3 is a type II transmembrane protein.
source: While it has been suggested that IFITM3 may adopt multiple topologies (Li et al., 2013; Yount et al., 2012), experimental evidence indicates that IFITM3 is a type II transmembrane protein characterized by the presence of a cytoplasmic-facing amino terminus, a CD225 domain consisting of a hydrophobic intramembrane (IM) domain, a cytoplasmic intracellular loop (CIL), and a hydrophobic transmembrane (TM) domain, and a very short carboxy terminus facing the vesicle lumen or extracellular space (Bailey et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PRRT2 adopts a similar topology to IFITM3 in membranes.
source: PRRT2 is thought to adopt a similar topology in membranes (Rossi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The GxxxG motif is conserved in IFITM3 of vertebrates.
source: The GxxxG motif is conserved in IFITM3 of vertebrates, indicating that it may play an important functional role (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The GxxxG motif is frequently associated with dimerization of membrane proteins.
source: The GxxxG motif, also known generally as a (small)xxx(small) motif, is frequently associated with dimerization of membrane proteins (Teese and Langosch, 2015; Overton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GxxxG motif has been described to drive oligomerization from cytoplasmic loops or linkers.
source: Most often shown to mediate pairing of hydrophobic transmembrane helices within a bilayer, the motif has also been described to drive oligomerization from cytoplasmic loops or linkers (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: IFITM3 WT-FLAG and mutants reach similar levels following transient transfection as determined by flow cytometry.
source: Transiently expressed IFITM3 mutants reached similar levels as wild-type (WT) as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The G91L mutant exhibits a significant expression defect by western blot analysis following transient transfection.
source: However, western blot analysis revealed a significant expression defect for the G91L mutant, but not for the others (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: In stably transfected cells, all IFITM3 constructs result in protein expression levels that exceed those observed following transient transfection.
source: In stably transfected cells, all IFITM3 constructs resulted in protein expression levels that exceeded those observed following transient transfection, and the only mutant exhibiting significantly reduced levels was G95W (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: G95W is the only mutant exhibiting significantly reduced expression levels in stably transfected cells.
source: In stably transfected cells, all IFITM3 constructs resulted in protein expression levels that exceeded those observed following transient transfection, and the only mutant exhibiting significantly reduced levels was G95W (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: IFITM3 WT is detected in early endosomes, late endosomes, and at the plasma membrane.
source: As shown previously (Shi et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2011; Feeley et al., 2011), IFITM3 WT was detected in early endosomes, late endosomes, and at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Approximately 30% of IFITM3 WT is associated with early endosomes.
source: Specifically, approximately 30% of IFITM3 WT was associated with early endosomes and 30% was associated with late endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 30% of IFITM3 WT is associated with late endosomes.
source: Specifically, approximately 30% of IFITM3 WT was associated with early endosomes and 30% was associated with late endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G91L, G95L, and G95W mutations do not obviously alter colocalization between IFITM3 and endosomes.
source: The G91L, G95L, and G95W mutations did not obviously alter colocalization between IFITM3 and endosomes in either stably or transiently transfected cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: IFITM3 WT strongly protects cells from IAV infection.
source: IFITM3 WT strongly protected cells from infection, but G91L resulted in a partial loss of virus restriction while G95L and G95W resulted in a more substantial loss of restriction (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: G91L results in a partial loss of IAV restriction.
source: IFITM3 WT strongly protected cells from infection, but G91L resulted in a partial loss of virus restriction while G95L and G95W resulted in a more substantial loss of restriction (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: G95L and G95W result in a more substantial loss of IAV restriction.
source: IFITM3 WT strongly protected cells from infection, but G91L resulted in a partial loss of virus restriction while G95L and G95W resulted in a more substantial loss of restriction (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The extent of IAV restriction does not correlate with relative levels of IFITM3 protein in stable cell lines.
source: The extent of restriction did not correlate with relative levels of IFITM3 protein in stable cell lines (Figure 2B), demonstrating that differential antiviral activity is not due to differential protein expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing expression levels (Figure 2B) and antiviral activity (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Inhibition of HIV-VSV-G by IFITM3 constructs resembles inhibition of IAV.
source: Inhibition of HIV-VSV-G by the IFITM3 constructs resembled inhibition of IAV, in that G95L and G95W resulted in a substantial loss of restriction.
evidence: This is supported by virus-cell fusion assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: G91L only slightly impacts HIV-VSV-G restriction and its activity is not significantly different from WT.
source: G91L, however, only slightly impacted virus restriction and its activity was not significantly different from WT.
evidence: This is supported by virus-cell fusion assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Glycine-95 is a major determinant for the broad inhibition of virus entry by IFITM3.
source: Therefore, a rational approach identified glycine-95 to be a major determinant for the broad inhibition of virus entry by IFITM3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antiviral assays against IAV and HIV-VSV-G.

claim: IFITM3 performs an antiviral function in virus-producing cells by incorporating into virions and reducing viral glycoprotein abundance and function.
source: We and others have previously demonstrated that, in addition to preventing virus entry into naive target cells, IFITM3 performs another antiviral function in virus-producing (infected) cells by incorporating into virions, reducing viral glycoprotein abundance and function, and reducing the fusogenic potential of virions (Tartour et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2015; Tartour et al., 2017; Ahi et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2019; Compton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFITM3 WT reduces the infectivity of HIV-1.
source: IFITM3 WT reduced the infectivity of HIV-1, while G95L resulted in a partial loss of activity.
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: G95L results in a partial loss of activity in restricting HIV-1 virion infectivity.
source: IFITM3 WT reduced the infectivity of HIV-1, while G95L resulted in a partial loss of activity.
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: G91L completely abrogates the antiviral function of IFITM3 against HIV-1 virion infectivity.
source: Strikingly, G91L completely abrogated this antiviral function (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Transient expression of IFITM3 WT in virus-producing cells is accompanied by a partial loss of Env gp120 and gp41 in those cells.
source: The transient expression of IFITM3 WT in virus-producing cells was accompanied by a partial loss of Env gp120 and gp41 in those cells (Figure 3C) and in virions (Figure 3D) as previously reported (Yu et al., 2015; Ahi et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C-D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient expression of IFITM3 WT in virus-producing cells is accompanied by a partial loss of Env gp120 and gp41 in virions.
source: The transient expression of IFITM3 WT in virus-producing cells was accompanied by a partial loss of Env gp120 and gp41 in those cells (Figure 3C) and in virions (Figure 3D) as previously reported (Yu et al., 2015; Ahi et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C-D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient expression of G91L or G95L mutants does not result in reduced Env levels.
source: In contrast, transient expression of the G91L or G95L mutants did not result in reduced Env levels (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Env quantity in virions does not fully account for the restriction of HIV-1 virion infectivity by IFITM3.
source: Since the G91L and G95L mutations differentially impact the restriction of HIV-1 virion infectivity by IFITM3, it is therefore unlikely that Env quantity in virions fully accounts for this restriction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both mutants have similar Env levels but different effects on infectivity.

claim: The G91L and G95L mutations strongly impair the ability of IFITM3 to incorporate into virions.
source: However, we observed that the G91L and G95L mutations strongly impaired the ability of IFITM3 itself to incorporate into virions (Figure 3G), and the extent of virion incorporation correlated with the measured impact on HIV-1 infectivity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The extent of IFITM3 virion incorporation correlates with the measured impact on HIV-1 infectivity.
source: However, we observed that the G91L and G95L mutations strongly impaired the ability of IFITM3 itself to incorporate into virions (Figure 3G), and the extent of virion incorporation correlated with the measured impact on HIV-1 infectivity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing virion incorporation (Figure 3G) and infectivity (Figure 3B).

claim: The dual antiviral functions performed by IFITM3 are critically regulated by the GxxxG motif.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the dual antiviral functions performed by IFITM3 (early-stage inhibition of virus entry and late-stage inhibition of virion infectivity) are critically regulated by the GxxxG motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antiviral assays in target cells and virus-producing cells.

claim: The early-stage inhibition of virus entry by IFITM3 depends primarily on glycine-95.
source: Interestingly, the former function depends primarily on glycine-95, while the latter function depends more on glycine-91.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of G91L and G95L mutations on virus entry versus virion infectivity.

claim: The late-stage inhibition of virion infectivity by IFITM3 depends more on glycine-91.
source: Interestingly, the former function depends primarily on glycine-95, while the latter function depends more on glycine-91.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of G91L and G95L mutations on virus entry versus virion infectivity.

claim: Co-transfection of IFITM3 WT-YFP and IFITM3 WT-mCherry results in high levels of detectable FRET.
source: By comparison, IFITM3 WT-YFP and IFITM3 WT-mCherry co-transfection resulted in high levels of detectable FRET (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Introduction of the G91L mutation partially inhibits FRET.
source: Relative to WT, introduction of the G91L mutation partially inhibited FRET, while the G95L mutation had a much stronger effect, reducing FRET to near background levels (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The G95L mutation reduces FRET to near background levels.
source: Relative to WT, introduction of the G91L mutation partially inhibited FRET, while the G95L mutation had a much stronger effect, reducing FRET to near background levels (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Both glycine-91 and glycine-95 contribute to IFITM3 oligomerization, but glycine-95 is the major determinant.
source: These data suggest that both glycine-91 and glycine-95 contribute to IFITM3 oligomerization, but that glycine-95 is the major determinant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: FRET was measured for heterologous pairs (combining IFITM3 WT-YFP and G95L-mCherry, and vice versa) and the results were indicative of an intermediate degree of oligomerization.
source: FRET was also measured for heterologous pairs (combining IFITM3 WT-YFP and G95L-mCherry, and vice versa) and the results were indicative of an intermediate degree of oligomerization (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-transfection of IFITM3 WT-YFP and IFITM3 WT-mCherry results in significant decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 400 picoseconds).
source: Co-transfection of IFITM3 WT-YFP and IFITM3 WT-mCherry resulted in significant decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 400 picoseconds), consistent with IFITM3 oligomerization (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Co-transfection of G91L-YFP and G91L-mCherry results in partial decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 225 picoseconds).
source: Meanwhile, co-transfection of G91L-YFP and G91L-mCherry resulted in partial decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 225 picoseconds), while we observed only minor decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 70 picoseconds) when G95L-YFP and G95L-mCherry were examined.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-transfection of G95L-YFP and G95L-mCherry results in only minor decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 70 picoseconds).
source: Meanwhile, co-transfection of G91L-YFP and G91L-mCherry resulted in partial decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 225 picoseconds), while we observed only minor decreases in YFP lifetimes (averaging about 70 picoseconds) when G95L-YFP and G95L-mCherry were examined.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The F75A/F78A mutations do not affect IFITM3 oligomerization.
source: Within this experimental framework, we confirmed that the F75A/F78A mutations did not affect IFITM3 oligomerization, nor did mutations within the amphipathic helix (S61A/N64A/T65A) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations within the amphipathic helix (S61A/N64A/T65A) do not affect IFITM3 oligomerization.
source: Within this experimental framework, we confirmed that the F75A/F78A mutations did not affect IFITM3 oligomerization, nor did mutations within the amphipathic helix (S61A/N64A/T65A) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The antiviral potency of IFITM3 WT tagged with mCherry or YFP at the amino terminus is decreased by 20% compared to IFITM3 WT-FLAG.
source: The antiviral potency of IFITM3 WT tagged with mCherry or YFP at the amino terminus was decreased by 20% compared to IFITM3 WT-FLAG (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: IFITM3 G95L tagged with mCherry or YFP exhibits no antiviral activity.
source: Nonetheless, IFITM3 G95L tagged with mCherry or YFP exhibited no antiviral activity whatsoever, validating the utility of our fluorescently-tagged IFITM3 constructs for mechanistic studies.
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Internal placement of mCherry or YFP in IFITM3 results in a greater loss of antiviral activity compared to amino terminal placement.
source: We found that the internal placement of mCherry or YFP resulted in a greater loss of antiviral activity compared to the amino terminal placement of mCherry or YFP. Specifically, the constructs encoding mCherry or YFP internally lost more than 40% of their activity compared to a 20% loss exhibited by constructs encoding mCherry or YFP at the amino terminus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by IAV infection assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: IFITM3 WT constructs encoding internal mCherry and YFP are FRET competent.
source: For thoroughness, we tested the IFITM3 WT constructs encoding internal mCherry and YFP for FRET competence and found that oligomerization was apparent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Introduction of the G95L mutation into IFITM3 constructs with internal fluorophores results in decreased oligomerization.
source: Furthermore, introduction of the G95L mutation into these constructs resulted in decreased oligomerization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: IFITM3 WT-myc readily pulls down with IFITM3 WT-FLAG in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: We found that IFITM3 WT-myc readily pulled down with IFITM3 WT-FLAG, while pull down of G95L-myc with G95L-FLAG was diminished by approximately 50% (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Pull down of G95L-myc with G95L-FLAG is diminished by approximately 50% in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: We found that IFITM3 WT-myc readily pulled down with IFITM3 WT-FLAG, while pull down of G95L-myc with G95L-FLAG was diminished by approximately 50% (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Pairing IFITM3 WT-FLAG with G95L-myc results in an intermediate degree of oligomerization.
source: To address heteromultimerization between IFITM3 WT and IFITM3 G95L, we paired IFITM3 WT-FLAG with G95L-myc and the results were indicative of an intermediate degree of oligomerization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Membrane-extracted IFITM3 forms oligomers.
source: Therefore, membrane-extracted IFITM3 forms oligomers, but the G95L mutation reduces oligomerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The G95L mutation reduces oligomerization of membrane-extracted IFITM3.
source: Therefore, membrane-extracted IFITM3 forms oligomers, but the G95L mutation reduces oligomerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Two populations of IFITM3 oligomers, exhibiting sizes of approximately 300 and 480 kilodaltons, are observed by blue native PAGE.
source: Two populations of IFITM3 oligomers, exhibiting sizes of approximately 300 and 480 kilodaltons, were readily observed for IFITM3 WT-FLAG and, to a lesser extent, IFITM3 G95L-FLAG.
evidence: This is supported by blue native PAGE data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The largest IFITM3 oligomer (480 kilodaltons) is reduced by approximately 50% for IFITM3 G95L.
source: The largest (480 kilodaltons) was reduced by approximately 50% for IFITM3 G95L (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by blue native PAGE data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: A population of IFITM3 dimers (expected at approximately 30 kilodaltons) was not detected by blue native PAGE.
source: We did not detect a population of IFITM3 dimers (expected at approximately 30 kilodaltons), which may reflect the specific conditions under which blue native PAGE was performed here.
evidence: This is an observation from blue native PAGE experiments.

claim: Glycine-95 is necessary for efficient IFITM3 oligomer formation.
source: Therefore, glycine-95 is necessary for efficient IFITM3 oligomer formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple oligomerization assays.

claim: IFITM3 WT-mCherry is 2.14 times brighter than mCherry monomers on average.
source: On average, IFITM3 WT-mCherry was found to be 2.14 times brighter than mCherry monomers (Shaner et al., 2004; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by Number and Brightness analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: G95L-mCherry brightness is not significantly different than mCherry monomers (averaging 1.30 times brighter).
source: In contrast, G95L-mCherry brightness was not significantly different than mCherry monomers (averaging 1.30 times brighter).
evidence: This is supported by Number and Brightness analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both IFITM3 WT-mCherry and G95L-mCherry form assemblies that are up to five times brighter than mCherry monomers.
source: Furthermore, relative to mCherry monomers, both IFITM3 WT-mCherry and G95L-mCherry formed assemblies that were up to five times brighter, but IFITM3 WT-mCherry demonstrated a greater propensity to form these higher order oligomers (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by Number and Brightness analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IFITM3 WT-mCherry demonstrates a greater propensity to form higher order oligomers than G95L-mCherry.
source: Furthermore, relative to mCherry monomers, both IFITM3 WT-mCherry and G95L-mCherry formed assemblies that were up to five times brighter, but IFITM3 WT-mCherry demonstrated a greater propensity to form these higher order oligomers (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by Number and Brightness analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IFITM3 WT exists primarily as a dimer.
source: However, the fact that IFITM3 WT exhibits a mean brightness that is roughly twofold greater than IFITM3 G95L supports the notion that the former exists primarily as a dimer and the latter as a monomer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from Number and Brightness analysis.

claim: IFITM3 G95L exists primarily as a monomer.
source: However, the fact that IFITM3 WT exhibits a mean brightness that is roughly twofold greater than IFITM3 G95L supports the notion that the former exists primarily as a dimer and the latter as a monomer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from Number and Brightness analysis.

claim: IFITM3 forms dimers and higher order oligomers in membranes in a glycine-95-dependent fashion.
source: Together, these data suggest that IFITM3 forms dimers and higher order oligomers in membranes in a glycine-95-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple oligomerization assays.

claim: IFITM3 WT expression leads to significantly increased membrane order.
source: Using FliptR in HEK293T stably expressing IFITM3-FLAG, we found that IFITM3 WT expression led to significantly increased membrane order (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The IFITM3-induced enhancement of membrane order is similar to that achieved by addition of soluble cholesterol.
source: In fact, the IFITM3-induced enhancement of membrane order was similar to that achieved by addition of soluble cholesterol, while cholesterol depletion with methyl-beta-cyclodextrin resulted in profound decreases in membrane order (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cholesterol depletion with methyl-beta-cyclodextrin results in profound decreases in membrane order.
source: In fact, the IFITM3-induced enhancement of membrane order was similar to that achieved by addition of soluble cholesterol, while cholesterol depletion with methyl-beta-cyclodextrin resulted in profound decreases in membrane order (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cells expressing IFITM3 G95L do not exhibit increased membrane order.
source: In contrast to WT, cells expressing IFITM3 G95L did not exhibit increased membrane order (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IFITM3 WT expression results in significantly increased membrane order as measured by Laurdan.
source: Similar results were obtained using Laurdan, in that IFITM3 WT expression resulted in significantly increased membrane order while G95L did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Laurdan measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: IFITM3 G95L does not increase membrane order as measured by Laurdan.
source: Similar results were obtained using Laurdan, in that IFITM3 WT expression resulted in significantly increased membrane order while G95L did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Laurdan measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Membrane order enhancement tracks with a functionally competent form of IFITM3 but not with a loss-of-function mutant.
source: These data indicate that membrane order enhancement tracks with a functionally competent form of IFITM3 but not with a loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing membrane order measurements with antiviral activity.

claim: Amphotericin B was previously reported to overcome the antiviral activity of IFITM3, rendering cells stably expressing IFITM3 fully permissive to IAV.
source: This antimycotic polyene compound was previously reported to overcome the antiviral activity of IFITM3, rendering cells stably expressing IFITM3 fully permissive to IAV (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When Ampho B is added to cells expressing IFITM3 WT, increased membrane order is no longer observed.
source: When we added Ampho B to cells expressing IFITM3 WT, we no longer observed increased membrane order (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ampho B prevents restriction by IFITM3 of HIV pseudotyped with hemagglutinin from IAV.
source: Furthermore, in identically treated cells, Ampho B prevented restriction by IFITM3 of HIV pseudotyped with hemagglutinin (HA) from IAV (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by infection assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The capacity for Ampho B to overcome the antiviral activity of IFITM3 is linked to its ability to decrease membrane order.
source: These findings show, for the first time, that the capacity for Ampho B to overcome the antiviral activity of IFITM3 is linked to its ability to decrease membrane order.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between Ampho B's effects on membrane order and antiviral activity.

claim: The use of Ampho B as an interrogative tool reinforces the role played by membrane order in the antiviral mechanism of IFITM3.
source: Therefore, the use of Ampho B as an interrogative tool reinforced the role played by membrane order in the antiviral mechanism of IFITM3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with Ampho B.

claim: The amphipathic helix of IFITM3 is critical for the membrane order enhancement by IFITM3.
source: Since we previously reported a critical role for the amphipathic helix of IFITM3 in virus restriction (Chesarino et al., 2017), we tested whether the helix was also required for the enhanced membrane order observed in cells expressing IFITM3. Like the G95L mutant, a version of IFITM3 encoding S61A/N64A/T65A mutations in the amphipathic helix lost the ability to increase membrane order (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: IFITM3 encoding S61A/N64A/T65A mutations in the amphipathic helix loses the ability to increase membrane order.
source: Like the G95L mutant, a version of IFITM3 encoding S61A/N64A/T65A mutations in the amphipathic helix lost the ability to increase membrane order (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Oligomerization and the amphipathic helix are dual requirements for the antiviral functions of IFITM3.
source: Since the S61A/N64A/T65A mutations did not inhibit oligomerization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), our results identify oligomerization and the amphipathic helix as dual requirements for the antiviral functions of IFITM3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing oligomerization, membrane order, and antiviral activity data.

claim: Virus restriction by IFITM3 occurs through oligomerization-dependent membrane stiffening induced by the amphipathic helix.
source: Overall, these data strongly suggest that virus restriction by IFITM3 occurs through oligomerization-dependent membrane stiffening induced by the amphipathic helix.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Co-transfection of PRRT2 WT-YFP and PRRT2 WT-mCherry results in significant FRET.
source: We observed that co-transfection of PRRT2 WT-YFP and PRRT2 WT-mCherry resulted in significant FRET, demonstrating that PRRT2 oligomerizes in living cell membranes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PRRT2 oligomerizes in living cell membranes.
source: We observed that co-transfection of PRRT2 WT-YFP and PRRT2 WT-mCherry resulted in significant FRET, demonstrating that PRRT2 oligomerizes in living cell membranes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: FRET is significantly reduced for PRRT2 pairs containing G305W.
source: However, FRET was significantly reduced for pairs containing G305W (G305W-YFP and G305W-mCherry) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PRRT2 pairs containing G305W do not exhibit loss in YFP lifetimes relative to their WT counterparts.
source: Furthermore, pairs containing G305W did not exhibit loss in YFP lifetimes relative to their WT counterparts (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mutation of glycine-305 in PRRT2 results in loss of protein oligomerization.
source: These data suggest that mutation of glycine-305 in PRRT2 results in loss of protein oligomerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FRET-FLIM data for PRRT2.

claim: The divergent functions played by homologues IFITM3 and PRRT2 in the regulation of fusion processes are controlled by a common determinant.
source: Therefore, the divergent functions played by homologues IFITM3 and PRRT2 in the regulation of fusion processes are controlled by a common determinant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both proteins require their respective glycines in the GxxxG motif for oligomerization and function.

claim: IFITM3 intercepts vesicles carrying inbound virions and restricts their release into the cytoplasm.
source: Second, IFITM3 has been observed to intercept vesicles carrying inbound virions and to restrict their release into the cytoplasm, while viruses that are insensitive to IFITM3 evade its encounter (Suddala et al., 2019; Spence et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Viruses that are insensitive to IFITM3 evade its encounter.
source: Second, IFITM3 has been observed to intercept vesicles carrying inbound virions and to restrict their release into the cytoplasm, while viruses that are insensitive to IFITM3 evade its encounter (Suddala et al., 2019; Spence et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The subcellular localization of IFITM3 determines its specificity and potency.
source: Together with the previous demonstrations that the subcellular localization of IFITM3 determines its specificity and potency (Compton et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2012; Chesarino et al., 2014b), a 'proximity-based' mechanism presents itself in which IFITM3 interacts with and modifies host membranes needed by some viruses to fuse with cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A 'proximity-based' mechanism presents itself in which IFITM3 interacts with and modifies host membranes needed by some viruses to fuse with cells.
source: Together with the previous demonstrations that the subcellular localization of IFITM3 determines its specificity and potency (Compton et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2012; Chesarino et al., 2014b), a 'proximity-based' mechanism presents itself in which IFITM3 interacts with and modifies host membranes needed by some viruses to fuse with cells.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on previous studies and current findings.

claim: The proximity-based model accommodates the antiviral effect of IFITM3 inside viral lipid bilayers.
source: Importantly, this model accommodates the antiviral effect of IFITM3 inside viral lipid bilayers as well (Tartour et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2015; Ahi et al., 2020; Suddala et al., 2019; Compton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An alanine scanning approach led to the identification of phenylalanine-75 and phenylalanine-78 as important for IFITM3 oligomerization in cell lysates.
source: Previously, an alanine scanning approach led to the identification of two residues (phenylalanine-75 and phenylalanine-78) that were important for IFITM3 oligomerization in cell lysates (John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Alanine mutagenesis overlapping glycine-91 or glycine-95 led to loss of stable protein expression.
source: This study did not functionally test a role for glycine-91 or glycine-95 in the oligomerization of IFITM3 because alanine mutagenesis overlapping these residues apparently led to loss of stable protein expression (Appourchaux et al., 2019; John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: F75A and F78A mutations disrupt antiviral activity.
source: While it has been confirmed that F75A and F78A mutations disrupt antiviral activity (Suddala et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018), IFITM3 oligomerization was not impacted by these mutations when assessed by FRET in living cells (Winkler et al., 2019) and we confirm here that F75A and F78A mutations do not interfere with the measurement of IFITM3 oligomerization by FRET.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and FRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: G91L partially abrogates oligomerization.
source: Instead, we find that G91L partially abrogates oligomerization while G95L almost completely disrupts oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: G95L almost completely disrupts oligomerization.
source: Instead, we find that G91L partially abrogates oligomerization while G95L almost completely disrupts oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: G95L strongly reduces the antiviral potential of IFITM3.
source: Moreover, our data shows that G95L strongly reduces the antiviral potential of IFITM3 as well as its capacity to increase membrane order (reduce membrane fluidity).
evidence: This is supported by antiviral assays shown in Figure 2 and membrane order measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: G95L reduces the capacity of IFITM3 to increase membrane order.
source: Moreover, our data shows that G95L strongly reduces the antiviral potential of IFITM3 as well as its capacity to increase membrane order (reduce membrane fluidity).
evidence: This is supported by membrane order measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The membrane stiffening property of IFITM3 is a strict correlate of its antiviral functions in cells and, perhaps, in virions.
source: Even though the exact mechanism by which Ampho B impacts mammalian membranes is unclear (Lin et al., 2013; Kamiński, 2014), these results identify that the membrane stiffening property of IFITM3 is a strict correlate of its antiviral functions in cells and, perhaps, in virions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with Ampho B and membrane order measurements.

claim: Glycine-91 and glycine-95 of the GxxxG motif are important for restriction of HIV-1 virion infectivity by IFITM3.
source: We found that glycine-91 and glycine-95 of the GxxxG motif were also important for restriction of HIV-1 virion infectivity by IFITM3.
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: The G91L mutation has a stronger impact than G95L on the restriction of HIV-1 infectivity in virus-producing cells.
source: However, the G91L mutation had a stronger impact than G95L on this antiviral activity in virus-producing cells, suggesting that IFITM3 oligomerization is not as crucial for the restriction of HIV-1 infectivity as it is for the restriction of incoming virus in target cells.
evidence: This is supported by HIV-1 infectivity assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: IFITM3 oligomerization is not as crucial for the restriction of HIV-1 infectivity as it is for the restriction of incoming virus in target cells.
source: However, the G91L mutation had a stronger impact than G95L on this antiviral activity in virus-producing cells, suggesting that IFITM3 oligomerization is not as crucial for the restriction of HIV-1 infectivity as it is for the restriction of incoming virus in target cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of G91L and G95L on different antiviral functions.

claim: De novo HIV-1 assembly occurs at the plasma membrane of virus-producing cells.
source: De novo HIV-1 assembly occurs at the plasma membrane of virus-producing cells, and this is the site where cellular IFITM3 is incorporated into virions (Compton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The majority of the FRET signal occurring between IFITM3-YFP and IFITM3-mCherry is detected in intracellular endosomes and other membrane vesicles.
source: Importantly, we noticed that the majority of the FRET signal occurring between IFITM3-YFP and IFITM3-mCherry was detected in intracellular endosomes and other membrane vesicles, while FRET at the cell surface was relatively low.
evidence: This is an observation from FRET-FLIM experiments.

claim: FRET at the cell surface between IFITM3-YFP and IFITM3-mCherry is relatively low.
source: Importantly, we noticed that the majority of the FRET signal occurring between IFITM3-YFP and IFITM3-mCherry was detected in intracellular endosomes and other membrane vesicles, while FRET at the cell surface was relatively low.
evidence: This is an observation from FRET-FLIM experiments.

claim: IFITM3 oligomers may be more abundant in endosomal membranes.
source: Therefore, IFITM3 oligomers may be more abundant in endosomal membranes and this agrees with our finding that viruses entering cells via fusion with endosomes (such as IAV) are strongly restricted by IFITM3 oligomers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from FRET distribution and antiviral activity patterns.

claim: Viruses entering cells via fusion with endosomes (such as IAV) are strongly restricted by IFITM3 oligomers.
source: Therefore, IFITM3 oligomers may be more abundant in endosomal membranes and this agrees with our finding that viruses entering cells via fusion with endosomes (such as IAV) are strongly restricted by IFITM3 oligomers.
evidence: This is supported by antiviral assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Protein oligomerization of the transmembrane protein Mic10 is essential for its capacity to induce curvature in mitochondrial membranes.
source: It has been shown that protein oligomerization of the transmembrane protein Mic10 is essential for its capacity to induce curvature in mitochondrial membranes (Barbot et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in membrane order are often accompanied by changes in membrane curvature.
source: Furthermore, changes in membrane order are often accompanied by changes in membrane curvature (Vanni et al., 2014; Rangamani et al., 2014; Golani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane order and curvature alterations may underlie the restriction of virus fusion by IFITM3.
source: It is possible that these two alterations to host membranes underlie the restriction of virus fusion by IFITM3.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known relationship between membrane order and curvature.

claim: Amphipathic helices interact with and bend membranes.
source: Moreover, amphipathic helices are characterized to interact with and bend membranes (Giménez-Andrés et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The amphipathic helix of IFITM3 is critical for the membrane order enhancement by IFITM3.
source: Here, we show for the first time that the amphipathic helix of IFITM3 is critical for the membrane order enhancement by IFITM3.
evidence: This is supported by FliptR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Oligomerization 'activates' the membrane deforming activity of the amphipathic helix.
source: Since we also show that glycine-95 of the GxxxG motif is also required for membrane order enhancement, our data may suggest that oligomerization 'activates' the membrane deforming activity of the amphipathic helix, and as a result, its antiviral potential.
evidence: This is speculation based on the dual requirement for oligomerization and the amphipathic helix.

claim: Local insertion of multiple amphipathic helices into stretches of membrane may be required for inhibition of virus fusion.
source: It is possible that local insertion of multiple amphipathic helices into stretches of membrane is required for inhibition of virus fusion, and IFITM3 oligomers provide a means to fulfill that requirement.
evidence: This is speculation based on the relationship between oligomerization and antiviral activity.

claim: GxxxG motifs can mediate heteromultimerization with other proteins.
source: In addition to mediating dimerization or oligomerization of transmembrane proteins (homomultimerization), GxxxG motifs have also been described to affect the propensity for interaction with other proteins (heteromultimerization) (Teese and Langosch, 2015; Faingold et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GxxxG motif may govern which proteins IFITM3 interacts with and to what extent.
source: Therefore, the GxxxG motif may also govern which proteins IFITM3 interacts with and to what extent.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known properties of GxxxG motifs.

claim: IFITM3 has been described to bind with IFITM1 and IFITM2.
source: IFITM3 has been described to bind with IFITM1 and IFITM2, and it is interesting to consider how IFITM heteromultimers may contribute to antiviral protection of the cell (John et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: VAPA is a cholesterol trafficking regulator that has been described as an essential cofactor for the antiviral effects of IFITM3.
source: This list includes cholesterol trafficking regulator VAPA and the metalloproteinase ZMPSTE24, two proteins that have been described as essential cofactors for the antiviral effects of IFITM3 (Amini-Bavil-Olyaee et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ZMPSTE24 is a metalloproteinase that has been described as an essential cofactor for the antiviral effects of IFITM3.
source: This list includes cholesterol trafficking regulator VAPA and the metalloproteinase ZMPSTE24, two proteins that have been described as essential cofactors for the antiviral effects of IFITM3 (Amini-Bavil-Olyaee et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The G95L loss-of-function mutant could be used to rule in or rule out VAPA and cholesterol as players in the antiviral mechanism of IFITM3.
source: Since the former is associated with the tendency for IFITM3 to cause cholesterol overload in endosomes, the G95L loss-of-function mutant could be used to rule in or rule out VAPA and cholesterol as players in the antiviral mechanism of IFITM3.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.

claim: The naturally occurring G305W/R mutations found in patients with neurological dysfunction disrupt PRRT2 activity.
source: While glycine-95 is critical for the oligomerization and anti-fusion activity of IFITM3, we show that the homologous site in PRRT2, glycine-305, regulates its oligomerization as well. The naturally occurring G305W/R mutations found in patients with neurological dysfunction are known to disrupt PRRT2 activity, and our results here provide novel insight into how loss-of-function occurs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and FRET-FLIM data for PRRT2 shown in Figure 7.

claim: The presence of a shared GxxxG motif in IFITM3, PRRT2, and some other CD225 family members suggests that an ancestral CD225-containing protein performed an unknown function that required oligomerization.
source: Therefore, the presence of a shared GxxxG motif in IFITM3, PRRT2, and some other CD225 family members suggests that an ancestral CD225-containing protein performed an unknown function that required oligomerization.
evidence: This is speculation based on evolutionary conservation of the GxxxG motif.

claim: The GxxxG motif is not intact in human IFITM5 and IFITM10.
source: Interestingly, the GxxxG motif is not intact in human IFITM5 and IFITM10.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments.

claim: IFITM5 is involved in bone formation and exhibits some antiviral activity when expressed ectopically.
source: IFITM5 is involved in bone formation and exhibits some antiviral activity when expressed ectopically (Huang et al., 2011), while the function of IFITM10 is unknown (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The function of IFITM10 is unknown.
source: IFITM5 is involved in bone formation and exhibits some antiviral activity when expressed ectopically (Huang et al., 2011), while the function of IFITM10 is unknown (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All CD225 proteins may play roles in regulating membrane fusion processes in cells.
source: We wonder whether all CD225 proteins play roles in regulating membrane fusion processes in cells—only time and further experiments will tell.
evidence: This is speculation based on the shared features of CD225 proteins.

claim: PRRT2 interacts with cellular fusogens known as SNAREs in a glycine-305-dependent manner.
source: However, just as the GxxxG motif in IFITM3 may mediate both homo- and heteromultimerization, it has been reported that PRRT2 interacts with cellular fusogens known as soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) in a glycine-305-dependent manner (Coleman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Oligomerization of CD225 proteins may result in alteration of protein architecture and the display of novel docking sites for protein-protein interactions.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that oligomerization of CD225 proteins results in alteration of protein architecture and the display of novel docking sites for protein-protein interactions, allowing for expansion of their functional repertoire.
evidence: This is speculation based on the relationship between oligomerization and protein function.
